To date the Canadian inland fishermen, when selling their fish, have been in a relatively weak bargaining position, and if they did not like the prices offered for their fish all they could do was to threaten to quit. Mr. Speaker, I am endeavouring to do just that. I appreciate your comments and 1 shall try to relate my remarks to the amendment. It is my understanding that the government of Canada is setting up this marketing board, in co-operation with the provinces concerned, in order to assist the fishermen in the marketing of their products so that they received a better price. In my opinion, if this board is to meet with any measure of success, it will require the complete co-operation of all the fishermen concerned.
This is a statement of fact borne out by events in every other industry. If I may give an example, at the present time there is a slowdown in mail deliveries in the Post Office Department. When labour is unhappy over wages or terms of employment it goes on strike, and we see a complete shutdown of the particular industry.
For these reasons we believe that the inland fishermen must be guaranteed a place on the board of directors of this marketing corporation as well as on the advisory board of the corporation. There is no provision in the bill to guarantee that the fishermen will be represented on the board. In our view one way to make sure that the fishermen will be behind the board is to guarantee their representation on the board. After all, if things do not go according to plan it will be fishermen themselves who will be the most seriously affected.
These are not my views alone; they were endorsed by the Minister without Portfolio when he spoke before the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on January 28. At one point he said that he is fully on record in the house a number of times as indicating there should be adequate representation from the fishermen's groups on the advisory committee. Even the Mclvor Commission report recommends that the membership of the board provide adequate representation of regional interests. I submit that one can rightly interpret regional interests in this matter to be directly applicable to the fishermen concerned. For these reasons I hope that the government will give favourable consideration to our amendments concerning actual representation of fishermen on the board of directors, and on the advisory board of this corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I shall try to confine my remarks to the substance of the amendment before us. I think the amendment is rather important, though I must confess, as it is written and as I try to relate it to the rest of clause 3, it is rather difficult to understand it clearly. Nevertheless, as I say, I believe it to be an important amendment, because if there is to be established a board of directors for this Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, I think it is essential and certainly worth while that at least some members of the board of directors be actively engaged in the industry itself.
As I construe the intent of the amendment moved by the previous speaker, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), it would seem that he is proposing in the amendment that of the members of the board of directors, which consists of nine persons, four be appointed from among those who are actually fishermen. If that is the intent of the hon. member's amendment, I think it ought to be supported.
On the other hand, if he is going beyond that and suggesting that a majority of the members, or that every member except the chairman or president of the board be chosen from those engaged in fishing, then it would seem to me a rather impractical proposition. Therefore I will proceed on the assumption that the hon. member is suggesting that three

or four members of the board of directors be selected from among those who are actively engaged in the industry as fishermen, and I would support the amendment on that basis.
I also think it is important that there at least be some representation of those engaged as fishermen on the board of directors, inasmuch as the board will, in a sense, be operating with and spending money that is really the fishermen's money. I understand that there will perhaps be an establishment grant in the order of $100,000 paid by the federal government and each of the three provinces, which will be contributing on a prorated basis, such as $50,000 federal and $25,000 from each of the three provinces, or some proportion of that sort.
Once the $100,000 establishment grant from the federal and provincial governments has been received, all of the operating expense of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Board will come out of the proceeds of the corporation's operations, which in turn will be derived from the production of the fishermen themselves. Therefore, if the money of these fishermen is going to be spent in operating the board and paying its administrative costs and salaries, it seems only logical that the fishermen be granted some direct say at the board of directors level.
The minister may well reply that provision is made later on in the bill, in clause 18 or so, to enable the minister to establish an advisory board consisting of 14 or 15 persons. It may well be that the minister may want to select five, six, seven or eight of the 15 members of this advisory board from among those who are actually engaged in fishing. But it is interesting to note that there is nothing specific in the legislation that provides that the advisory board shall necessarily have fisher-men-producers actually on the board. It seems to me that the minister would want to agree that the legislation should make some specific provision to include fishermen on the advisory board.
It may be that there will be a number of fishermen on the advisory board but I would insist that there be at least 2, 3 or 4, some small number such as that-I would not want to go beyond that figure for practical reasons-on the membership of the board of directors itself. I do not know what arguments the minister would advance in opposition to this amendment, but we shall soon find out.

I have also one further argument to advance in support of the contention that there be some fishermen among the membership of the board of directors. There is a tendency, human nature being what it is, for boards or administrative bodies to start making free with other people's money. We can see how that has happened with the Canadian Wheat Board. One can see it happening with boards of directors of private corporations. Once set up boards of directors or similar administrative bodies establish themselves in lavishly furnished headquarter offices and they do not stint on the trappings that go with administrative offices. I feel that such a tendency toward extravagance would be curtailed if on the board to be set up one or two actual producers or fishermen were included. Their presence on the board might restrain any tendency toward extravagance by other board members. I think this is a concrete argument, and I believe there should be provision in this bill for the inclusion of two or three producers or fishermen on the board to be set up.
I will say no more, Mr. Speaker, because I am interested to hear the remarks of the Minister without Portfolio. I hope he will support the amendment.

It is important for hon. members to understand, Mr. Speaker, that under the legislation responsibility for fish marketing is to pass from the private sector of our community to a corporate body set up by various governments. The amendment provides that on the body to be set up there shall be fishermen representative of Canada. Fishermen from various parts of Canada will be asked to serve on the board.
As the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) indicated, the amendment before the house was one of the amendments moved in committee. It did not pass in committee. I will not take up the time of the house by explaining in detail what happened in committee; it is enough for me to say that if hon. members read the committee proceedings they will see how totally inadequate is our

present committee stage in the legislative process.
The proposed amendment seeks to make certain that active fishermen are appointed to the board. The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) said, "Oh, you can take my word for it. On this corporate body there will be representatives of fishermen. I give you my guarantee that this will be so.'' We wanted a commitment of this kind from the minister so that the fishermen of Ontario, the prairie provinces and other parts of Canada would know they are going to be represented on the corporate body. As I say, the minister gave his word, or we interpreted his remarks to mean that he had given his word. In view of that commitment we thought the minister would support the amendment that has been moved. Unfortunately, in the discussions before the committee on this point we learned that the government does not intend to appoint fishermen to the board. We learned that they want on this corporate body people who are experts in marketing, in commercial aspects of fisheries, in finance, negotiations and so on. Although he had given his word, the minister turned around and argued that there was a need to appoint experts to the board and that fishermen might not be able to fulfil the requirements.
Another point which was raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier) was that fishermen were not well enough educated to occupy positions on the board. That remark left me thunderstruck. I was really taken by surprise.

On page 4 of Bill C-148 there is an indication of the purposes and powers of the proposed corporate body, which go far beyond the level of expertise that would indicate that the people in question would have to be marketing experts and financiers. All eight subclauses of clause 7 indicate that the purposes of the corporation takes in the whole gambit of the fishing operation. He said: Mr. Speaker, my comments this afternoon will be directed to Bill C-148, an act to establish the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, with special reference to the financial control of the corporation.
Clause 15 of the bill, for example, provides that the corporation is to be a corporation within the meaning of the Financial Administration Act. Clause 16 provides that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) may make grants to the corporation not exceeding in the aggregate $100,000 to enable the corporation to meet initial operating and establishment expenses, while under clause 17 the Governor in Council may authorize the Minister of Finance to guarantee and make loans to the corporation up to an amount which shall not exceed $5 million.
There is nothing in the bill, which I have read from cover to cover, about the books to be kept or who is responsible for the preparation of financial statements or who is responsible for auditing the accounts of the corporation. In the absence of any direction in the act, section 85 of the Financial Administration Act leaves the financial statements of the Crown corporation subject to such directions as to form as the Treasury Board may give, and states under section 77 (1) that where no provision has been made in any act for the appointment of an auditor the Governor in Council shall designate someone to serve as auditor.
I believe that the question therefore arises whether the Auditor General is to be appointed the sole auditor or a joint auditor in accordance with the recommendations made by the Public Accounts Committee in its

eighth report of 1964-65. I hope that the government will agree that it would be in the best interests of parliament in its control of public funds if the Auditor General were empowered to audit the accounts of all the Crown corporations, agencies and other public bodies which are owned or controlled by the Crown and report thereon to the house.
It is for this reason, therefore, that I move, seconded by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan), that the following amendment be incorporated into the act to regulate interprovincial and export trade in freshwater fish and to establish the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation:
That clause 17 be amended by adding thereto new subclause (3) as follows:
"The accounts and financial transactions of the Corporation shall be audited annually by the Auditor General."

We saw no Hollywood stars, in answer to my more youthful friend. I was impressed by the name "Isis A". While the Canadian scientists told us many things about this satellite, I did not hear from anyone a recollection of the mythological connection, which might indeed have been very appropriate.
Isis was one of the more, indeed for a long time, paramount goddesses of ancient Egypt. She was regarded as the daughter of the earth and sky. I thought this was a very appropriate name, although I know that Isis means something else. It is one of those initialled conglomerations which not only clutter the international jargon but the scientific jargon. I also recall, and this may not be estheti-cally very pleasing, that Isis was a horned goddess. The minister (Mr. Drury) will recall a certain anxiety about whether or not antennae would be projected from Isis A. They were projected and I assume everything is working fine, so we not only have the goddess Isis up there but it is appropriately a horned goddess. We are very proud of this operation, and I think Canadians can take pride in their scientific community.
February 7, 1969	COMMONS
I do not want to carry on too long on this quiet and friendly Friday afternoon because I know there will be other opportunities to discuss this matter when the bill setting up the Department of Communications, and the corporation are before us as well as committee discussions. However, there are as well as international obligations, domestic implications of a broad political nature which are of concern.
It has pained me that in recent weeks most of the discussions in the Canadian press about the whole question of satellites has dealt with argumentation and disagreement between governments representing the provinces and the dominion. The last thing I should like to do at this time or at any time is to say anything which might exacerbate differences within this country. I recognize, as any thoughtful resident of a federal state must recognize, that this is a very difficult question. There is no argument that the dominion responsibility in the field of the development and projection of satellites is clear. I agree with the white paper, the author of which is sitting opposite me, and the statement that the government is responsible for the international negotiations concerned with communications satellites, both domestic and international. I also agree with the statement that the government is the only body which can negotiate with other countries in this field and that the relationship between domestic communications satellites and the national interest is of vital and unique importance. This must be made unmistakably clear.
I think this is a propitious statement; indeed, perhaps an axion of international relations in this country which we can accept. Yet-this is the complexity of a federal state -that the content of satellite programs would in part be educational and cultural. They are not purely appraisors of weather data. Education and culture would be very important parts of the larger payload, to use another bit of jargon I have been picking up. That this is the concern, indeed the jurisdiction, if I may use that word, of provinces can hardly be denied. It is not surprising that some of the provinces are expressing an interest in this sophisticated, modern "razzle dazzle" vehicle of communications. The interest of one of the provinces has been expressed over a long period of time. Therefore, it should be no surprise that the province of Quebec has more than a passing interest in this particular question.

It was a long time ago that Premier Bertrand, speaking in Hull, said:
We want an integrated and complete system embracing not only education and culture, but also the transmission of data and exchanges among knowledge banks.
It is in this perspective that we have turned to communication satellites. Efficiency demands that we control this integrated system in its entirety, but this will not inhibit co-operation and exchanges with the other provinces and with the federal government, if such is to be.
This is a field in which Quebec must act if Quebeckers are to feel that their culture and their own particular genius can be put to use not only in the field of arts and letters, but also in that of science and technology.
This statement was made a long time ago, and there have been others. Therefore, we would have to observe that Quebec's interest is not something of recent vintage. Mr. Cardinal in his discussions with the officers, and indeed the officer, of the Republic of France a few days ago was not breaking new ground. One cannot, and certainly I do not, applaud all that Mr. Cardinal said or did in that particular context. I would suggest that consultation with the dominion government should have taken place before the initialling of agreements or the signing of letters of intent.
I think that a nation state must be the only vehicle for the expression of international personality. Yet as one who is concerned with all of Canada and its provinces, I cannot refrain from asking other questions. One asks what has happened to the old idea of co-operative federalism, as we used to call it. I am interested in the pattern of consultation which has been reported for some time. The Foreign Secretary of France and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau), held discussions in Quebec. The Foreign Secretary of France and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) have had what are described as long and cordial discussions at the United Nations, with satellites as part of the agenda. Technicians of France are in Canada working in co-operation with our scientific people. There is an exchange of, and I note this, not educators but technicians between Quebec and France. But where in all of this pattern is the co-operation, or discussion between the other two members of the triangle? When do Quebec and Canada get together? When do Ottawa and Quebec city engage in a dialogue? This is, I submit, a very, very important question.
On November 26 before, I am sure, a large and enthusiastic television audience, the

5292	COMMONS
Canadian Overseas Telecommunications minister-designate of communications said that we were going to sit down and talk to Quebec about this problem of a province like Quebec getting involved with foreign governments in the creation of a satellite. I make that remark parenthetically. When he was asked when he was going to do this, his answer was, "Right away".
One asks, were these discussions held? What was the result? The cool, polite statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the cool and, I think, polite response of Mr. Cardinal lead me to ask when these chats took place and how effective they were. Surely, in Canada there should be no barrier of silence between federal and provincial people on this or any other matter. It would be a strange flaw in communications if this were the case. I feel very deeply that the advanced technology which makes communications satellites possible in this wonderfully advanced and, in some ways, highly enlightened age, should be a great agency for unity, for closer relations between the peoples not just of one country but indeed between countries. How dreadful it would be if this modern device and this modern expansion of man's capacity to communicate should in our own country become a vehicle, not for harmonious and strengthened communications, but of discord and disunity.
I am anxious to see this country go forward in its satellite program. I have immense confidence, and indeed pride, in the advances made by some of our scientific people. I note with the greatest approval the participation of the university field in this branch of the sciences. I have every confidence in the corporation which we are now discussing. I am sure that all of these people can do the technical job, but we must make sure that the broader political decisions are made thought-full and in time.
There is much more that I could say, and in weeks hence perhaps I shall have a chance to do so. When we get into committee we may submit, for the consideration of the committee and eventually the house, an improvement to clause 3 of the bill. I wonder whether a raising of the ceiling figures set out there, and thereby the assurance of getting parliamentary control where it should be, coupled with a vote of confidence in the corporation to discharge operations far in excess of the small amount set out at the present time, might not be a better way of dealing with the matter. I think this is something we would ask the committee to consider.

I want to end as I began, Mr. Speaker, by expressing great support for the work done by the C.O.T.C. and the hope that it will be a useful vehicle for greater activity. We will be interested to hear whether any plans have been made for its use in the domestic satellite program, despite the word "external" in the bill. We shall be urging, as we have in recent weeks, that the Canadian public be more fully informed on what is in store for this particular aspect of communications. It is costly; it is important; it is sensitive. There are involvements international and domestic which are most acute. I think there is no better way of guaranteeing public support and understanding than by full, ample and prompt communication.

Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker, the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), expressed the hope that he could set the tone for a particularly dispassionate debate this Friday afternoon on the propositions contained in Bill S-5. There is no doubt that the hon. member has succeeded in setting such a tone. Perhaps because the hon. member is a friendly sort of person-very analytical, too, I might add- he has succeeded in doing this. But I suspect there is a second reason, namely, that the bill before us is quite non-controversial. As I see it, there are two provisions contained in Bill S-5.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
One is to delete the special reference to Newfoundland in the operations of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation. Even though the hon. member for Hillsborough and the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) are in some disagreement as to whether or not Newfoundland is unique in Canada in being an overseas province, I will stay out of that argument. Neither do I know whether Prince Edward islanders really consider that province to be an island in the same sense as is Newfoundland.
I also read the comments made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) on February 3 when he spoke on this bill. I agree that perhaps it is time the spending authority of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation be revised. I am not sure, however, that the minister should be proposing to remove the limitations completely and to vest in the cabinet the limiting power by way of the Governor in Council.

February 7, 1969	COMMONS
I would have preferred an amendment whereby the ceilings would have been increased substantially from $50,000, which was the limit set in one case, and $5,000 which was the limit in another case. I think it would have been better to increase these limitations substantially but without removing them from the statute. I do not know how significant it will be to transfer the limiting power relative to this corporation from parliament into the hands of the Governor in Council. Inasmuch as members of the cabinet and the Governor in Council are responsible to parliament, it really works out to the same thing.
I would like to take the opportunity, as has the hon. member for Hillsborough, to make some reference to our domestic communication space satellite plans and program. I do not agree with the hon. member that we would be making a mistake if we engaged in the construction of a Canadian built communication space satellite. As I understand the remarks of the hon. member, he seemed to be of the opinion that if such a space communication system were to be developed by Canada, and if it were to cost us in excess of $70 or $80 million, this might well be too high a price to pay. He suggested that perhaps we should look to the United States to provide us with such a satellite at a reduced price.
I feel that because of the advantages which could accrue to our scientific community in the building of an even greater scientific expertise, it would be worth the price for us to build a communications space satellite capability in Canada, even if the cost does rise to the level estimated by the Postmaster General. As I understood him, he estimates the cost to be in the neighbourhood of $70 million to $100 million. It is often said that one of the advantages that a country derives from military conflict, and this is rather ironic and sad, is that at least at that time scientific expertise and technological competence surges forward and increases rapidly. I should like to think that in our time man can, through peaceful scientific programs of endeavour, increase his expertise and technological ability without having to resort to warfare in order to do so. So, I emphasize that I would consider it very sad if, for the purpose of saving a few million dollars, we decided to buy a communication space satellite from some other country. I am sure that in so doing we would be relegating our Canadian scientific community to the background and the repercussions from that would be felt for many years.

I say to the minister, let us by all means go full speed ahead with the plans for the construction and development of a Canadian space communication satellite capability.
I also want to bring to the minister's attention the fact that, as I read his comments when he introduced this bill, he gave us to understand that within a relatively short time from now Canada would be constructing a second ground receiving station in Nova Scotia in order to take advantage to a greater degree of the programs that are receivable from the Intelsat Atlantic satellites. I do not know exactly how many Intelsat satellites are in orbit over the Atlantic region in Canada and Europe, but I do know that in recent days Intelsat has launched a communications satellite in the Pacific region. To the best of my knowledge, Canada does not yet have a ground receiving station on the west coast. As I interpret the situation, this means that Canada cannot avail itself of any communication receivable through the Intelsat Pacific region satellite, and yet we are paying for it.
Canada is a member of Intelsat and pays 5 or 6 per cent of the cost of that organization. However, we are not able to make any use of whatever facilities Intelsat has in the Pacific region because we have not yet established a ground receiving station there. It seems to me the minister should explain at an early date why the policy is to go ahead with the building of a second ground receiving station on the east coast while at the same time we are not building the first one on the Pacific coast. I think that is a valid point which the minister might want to deal with at some future date.
The hon. member for Hillsborough, in his remarks relative to this bill, also made some mention of the fact that there was a consortium in Europe attempting to develop a launching capability to send up a Franco-German space satellite and that Quebec would be involved in this venture. About two months ago I asked the minister if he could indicate whether the province of Quebec was really serious about the building of a ground receiving station somewhere in the province which would be capable of receiving signals from the Franco-German satellite. Perhaps the minister was not in a position to reply at that time, but since then there have been some developments. Quebec seems to be determined to build such a ground receiving station with or without federal assistance. There is a rumour that direct assistance will be given to the province of Quebec by the government of France. I would not attempt to go

Although I did not have the pleasure of attending with other members of parliament about a week or ten days ago the launching of Isis at Vandenburg Air Force Base, I did have the opportunity about two months ago of attending the meetings of the Canada-France Parliamentary Association in France. While there we were invited to view the scientific space communications satellite development program, and we were taken on a tour of the Centre National des Etudes Spatiales just outside Paris. Judging from some of the comments that I heard at that time, there seems to be an equal determination somehow to bring the province of Quebec into that program. I wish the minister the best of luck in the days ahead in his attempts to cope with that thorny constitutional problem.
I conclude by saying that so far as the specific provisions of Bill S-5 are concerned, there is nothing at all to which to object. I merely wish to register a small caveat. Perhaps, instead of removing entirely the statutory limit on the spending power of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation and leaving it within the discretion of Treasury Board or the Governor in Council, it would have been better to have revised the amount upwards substantially, from $50,000 to, say, $1 million, or from $5,000 in the case of long term leases to an amount of four or five times that. With those comments, I feel that I have at least had my say so far as Canadian communications policy is concerned.

Further, I do not think authority should be delegated in such a general way. Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for their constructive approach to this bill and for their co-operative attitude. I wish to reassure hon. members opposite that I share with them the desire that our future satellite should be developed in Canada and, as far as possible, manufactured in this country.
Several hon. members mentioned what is really one point. I suppose it could be taken up in committee but I thought I would explain the matter to them now. I agree that we should raise the rather unrealistic limits now imposed by the act on the directors of the corporation. Raising those limits to $200,000 say, or $500,000 would constitute an appreciable improvement. There is no question about that. But I emphasize that this would not eliminate the need for future amendments to be brought before the house if conditions were so to dictate. It must be remembered that in this country we have two pieces of legislation that must be considered, the government contracts regulations and our financial regulations. If we raised the limit as has been suggested, the C.O.T.C. would remain an exception to the financial control mechanism prescribed by the Financial Administration Act with respect to all other government departments and agencies. It might further be noted that the C.O.T.C. is listed in the schedule of government departments and agencies to which this act should apply. Thus, we would have an existing inconsistency in legislation, which would really be a misalignment.
Section 22 of government contracts regulations provides that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, on the recommendation of Treasury Board prescribe the limits to transactions that may be entered into without approval. Perhaps I ought to read that section, which is as follows:
22. Notwithstanding anything in these Regulations, the Treasury Board may, in respect of a particular contracting authority, upon notification to the contracting authority, increase or decrease any one or more of the amounts specified in Parts I, II, III and IV.
February 7. 1969
5296	COMMONS DEBATES
Canadian Overseas Telecommunications
Part I deals with construction contracts; Part II with purchase contracts; Part III with service contracts and Part IV with leases.
The proposed amendment will remove the existing limits which, as was explained on February 3 and again today, are considered unreasonable. Secondly, it brings C.O.T.C. under the financial control mechanism the federal government has instituted in respect of government departments and agencies as prescribed by the Financial Administration Act. Section 39 of that act reads as follows:
39. The Governor in Council may make regulations with respect to the conditions under which contracts may be entered into and, notwithstanding any other Act,
a)	may direct that no contract by the terms of which payments are required in excess of such amount or amounts as the Governor in Council may prescribe shall be entered into or have any force or effect unless entry into the contract has been approved by the Governor in Council or the Treasury Board, and
b)	may make regulations with respect to the security to be given to and in the name of Her Majesty to secure the due performance of contracts.
What we are really doing here is bringing the C.O.T.C. into the financial structure governing the activities of all other departments of government or agencies. In other words, the C.O.T.C. will not be an orphan. I think we have all the control we want through appropriate institutions which have been set up and through structures as outlined and detailed in legislation to which I just referred. I simply want to place that fact before hon. members.
Before concluding my remarks, may I move that the motion for second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications of Bill S-5, an act to amend the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation Act be amended by substituting for the words "Standing Committee on Transport and Communications" the words, "Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts".

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, December 19, the motion of Mr. Wahn for second reading of Bill S-ll, to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada.

On December 19, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) sponsored Bill S-ll which
Private Bills
is an act to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada. After a very erudite exposition of this particular company he made the remark that he was ready to answer questions. I note with sadness that he is not in the house this afternoon because we in the New Democratic Party have many questions to be answered before this bill is finally passed.
He is derelict in his duty.

I notice other hon. members who have sponsored similar bills are here. I hope they will listen attentively and absorb some of the remarks I will make, then pass them along to the hon. member for St. Paul's.
Bill S-ll, Mr. Speaker, is an act to incorporate Aetna Casualty Company of Canada and sets forth in the incorporation the names of some very successful lawyers as well as an insurance agent.
The capital stock of the company shall be $5 million divided into shares of $50 each. The amount to be subscribed before the general meeting for the election of officers is called shall be $500,000. When this particular bill was before the Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce on October 23, counsel for the company stated that the Aetna Life and Casualty Company is the parent company of Aetna Life Insurance Company of Hartford and the Aetna Casualty Insurance Company of Hartford. One would find that rather difficult to follow, Mr. Speaker, unless you have a full appreciation of the corporate conglomeration that prevails in our society.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The company has a wide, horizontal and vertical base not only in the United States of America but also in Canada. They have operated in Canada for approximately 49 years. This is an attempt to incorporate a company dealing in all classes of insurance other than that of life. You will notice in clause 6 of the bill an enumeration of the classes of insurance in which it hopes to participate. It goes from the letter "A" to the letter "Z" which would indicate there are 26 classes of insurance. I have heard it said that when it comes to a matter of security we should have security from the womb to the tomb. Here, we have insurance from "A" to a "Z" which is quite a remarkable expansion by this company.
Last week, Mr. Speaker, I happened to see the picture "2001 A.D.", which dealt with the problems of space. I looked in this bill to

see if there was any reference to outer space insurance and I noticed there was not. I would ask hon. members on the other side to bring this lack to the attention of the sponsor of the bill. In the near future young men will be flying to the moon, and I would like to think that some company would have outer space insurance.
It would be rather interesting to you, Mr. Speaker, to hear an enumeration of the particular types of insurance in which this company will engage. They are fire insurance, accident insurance, aircraft insurance, automobile insurance, boiler insurance, credit insurance, earthquake insurance, explosion insurance, falling aircraft insurance, forgery insurance, guarantee insurance, hail insurance, impact by vehicles insurance, inland transportation insurance, livestock insurance, machinery insurance, marine insurance, personal property insurance, plate glass insurance, real property insurance, sickness insurance, sprinkler leakage insurance, theft insurance, water damage insurance, weather insurance and windstorm insurance. The list is quite impressive.
This brings me to the main thrust of my remarks. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that just in the past week or two we had an application from a company called Excelsior Life Insurance, and I notice that this company has a 70 per cent interest in Excelsior Life Insurance.
We have an American owned company having a 70 per cent control of a Canadian insurance company called Excelsior Life, and now it wants to incorporate another company to cover all forms of insurance with the exception of life insurance. I would imagine it thinks it can use Excelsior Life Insurance Company to take care of its insurance holdings.
In his opening remarks, the sponsor of the bill pleaded with members of the house to consider that even though it was American capital that was setting up this company the employee content would be Canadian. In a rather tender plea, he suggested that the intention of the company is to have its profits remain in Canada for Canadian use. When I say that is a tender plea, it makes me realize that the profits of this particular company in Canada, with regard to this same type of business under a different name, amounted to $785,000 for the year 1967, a substantial amount.
In the Banking and Commerce Committee one of the able Senators asked how many

Canadian shareholders there were in this company. After a little examination and huddling together by those concerned, they suggested that there were 300 Canadian shareholders. In the Aetna Insurance Company, which is an American company, there are
25,000	shareholders, and here we have a Canadian content of 300 Canadian shareholders.
In days like these, when you have takeover bids by American companies for Canadian insurance companies, I would have thought the government would have brought an immediate halt to the incorporation of companies which are American owned until it made a full examination of this take-over problem. Remember, Mr. Speaker, during the last week one of our big Canadian insurance firms attempted to mutualize its company to avoid an American take-over. When I speak of mutualization, I refer directly to the ownership of that company being in the hands of Canadian shareholders. This is what mutualization means.
The bid for mutualization with regard to that particular company failed. Now, it has exposed itself to the strong winds of American companies with regard to the take-over of Canadian life and other insurance companies. If the sponsor of this bill and some of the hon. members on the other side of the house realized the impact and import of this attempt by American companies to take over and dominate the insurance field, I am sure they would rise to their feet and ask that the government take immediate steps to stop this intrusion into our economy.
What action did the government take in this matter?

The hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) has brought forth a very salient point. He asks what action did the government take. I am sorry to say members of the government performed as usual. They just sat there and did nothing.
I recall that when I referred to the performance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the Commonwealth Conference as being a zero performance there was a great howl on the other side of the house. When I referred to the performance of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) in the task force on housing and said he had scored a double zero with regard to that important matter, there was another great howl. Here again we have a
February 7, 1969

fundamental issue with regard to the economy of our country and the government once more sits idly by and does nothing.
This is a sad commentary on this government that attempted to gain power in Canada on the supposition that they would be men of action, avant-garde men. This great leader, whom they elected at the party's leadership convention, would lead Canada into a position of strength and stability. Unfortunately, this has not happened.
Most Canadians are worried about American ownership in Canada. When I reiterate that Aetna Insurance Company has a 70 per cent interest in the Excelsior Insurance Company and has a broad base of insurance right through Canada and the United States, it brings to mind the wisdom and the experience of Walter Gordon. You, Mr. Speaker, remember the contemptible attitude that was taken by some members on the other side with regard to this outstanding Canadian who had a remarkable record in the financial affairs of our country, and who came to Ottawa with the hope that he would be able to lead Canada through these troubled times. He wrote a book which was well received, underlining the problems of foreign ownership. Here, we have a government that not only rejected his ideas but rejected the man himself.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I happened to read the recent book by Peter Newman called "The Distemper of Our Times". He sets forth the position of which Mr. Gordon attempted to make the Canadian public aware. It is rather unfortunate that Mr. Newman's book should have come out late in December at a time when another book by another Canadian personality came out, because the second book by that great woman of Canada-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It so happens that the book by Mr. Newman struck me so forcibly that I just had to bring it to your attention. So many members have not read that book, although they have read the other book by that gallant lady who sat on the other side.

At page 222 of his book Mr. Newman set forth the problem of foreign ownership. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the main burden of my remarks is with regard to foreign ownership. I noticed that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) looked up. This is rather important because he was the man who sponsored the Canada-U.S. auto pact or at least piloted it through the house. He knows what I am talking about when I mention the problem of foreign ownership. But he, like so many members of the cabinet, pretends to be unaware of the remarkable penetration of our economy that has taken place by the United States. I hope he does not take that attitude, but rather agrees with me there should be a task force set up to study the situation in respect of insurance companies in Canada. A study should be made of their ownership, the types of insurance they sell, the need for insurance companies, the use of capital by the insurance companies and the necessity for the allocation of the capital funds of these particular companies. I am sure he would agree with that general principle.
I should like to return to the matter of Mr. Newman's book because he has a very succinct and persuasive manner in his writing. He sets forth this problem in respect of foreign ownership. He refers to the report that was published by the task force set up to study foreign ownership and control in Canada. We now call it the Watkins report. At page 222 we read:
The report stressed that foreign investment is not simply the movement of capital between two countries, but also a political phenomenon. "Foreign control," it concluded, "means the potential shift outside the country of the locus of some types of decision-making. To the extent decision-making is eroded, national independence-being, in a broad sense, the ability to make decisions in the national interest-is reduced." It also warned about the use by foreign governments of the parent-subsidiary relationship as an instrument of their foreign policy. "The Canadian-based subsidiary," the report noted, "is confronted with two peaks of sovereignty; it must choose and might be expected to defer to the higher peak. In the nature of the case, the higher peak will typically be the home country."
I mention that because of the remark made by the sponsor of the bill to the effect that the profits of this company would be retained in Canada. One always remembers the action of the United States government with regard to the equalization tax and the direction by the United States government that subsidiaries of United States companies operating in

February 7, 1969

Canada send back some of their profits to the United States to take care of the balance of payments problem. This appears to be a very serious problem in the United States, and we in Canada also have suffered in respect of the balance of payments problem. However persuasive the sponsor of this bill may have wanted to be with regard to the retention of profits in Canada, we are subject to the statement that a subsidiary of a United States company would have to act in accordance with United States law and the dictates of the parent company. This is an unfortunate happening. It is an unfortunate fact in the economic life of our country and throughout the world that any subsidiary branch plant operating in another company is subject to the direct control of the parent company.
This is the opening remark set forth in the statement by Mr. Newman. I shall read again this very interesting material of which all of us should be aware:
Gordon's complaints about the behaviour of foreign subsidiaries in Canada included such things as the absence of a minority Canadian interest in their equity stock distribution: little meaningful Canadian representation on these firms' boards of directors; the fact that export policies were set by parent organizations, often against the domestic Canadian interest; and the reluctance of most American firms to process their raw materials before shipping them to the United States-

Mr. Speaker, I was very interested in the remarks my friend was making at the time his 20 minutes expired. The argument he was developing was directed to the control of the Canadian economy by outside interests. A number of private bills such as this dealing with the insurance problem have been before us. Again, I shall ask a question which has been asked before. Just what is the government's position on this particular phase of our economy? Are we to take it for granted that it is government policy to allow the insurance field to be increasingly dominated by outside interests or are we to try to retain for Canada

a larger degree of control than we presently have?
It is interesting to read the reports of those in charge of the insurance department. They realize what is happening in the insurance field. This is really part of the financial structure of this country. Slowly but surely to a very large degree we have lost control of this particular sector of our economy. It is amazing that private members constantly bring these bills before the house. Sometimes I wonder whether they go back to their constituencies and tell the people who elected them that they are in favour of selling Canada lock, stock and barrel to foreign investors. That is exactly what is happening. Private bill after private bill is brought in by members who, in fact, are telling us and the Canadian public that they are in favour of taking another chunk of our Canadian economy and shipping it south of the border or to some other nation. They are in favour of shipping out of Canada the control of our economy.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This is the story we are trying to get across. This is the story we are trying to leave with the Canadian nation. It is time the government laid down a policy. This policy should not be left to a handful of private members who bring in these bills. The government gets out from under by saying such bills do not represent government policy, but only policy negotiated by members who happen to be in the Liberal party.
If these bills go through, and hon. members are hoping they will, another chunk of our economy will be going down the drain. Let us have a look at this specific bill. It is designed to incorporate the Aetna Casualty Company of Canada. I am not going to go over the arguments which other hon. members have put before this house. The control of this company is completely held in the United States. Just last week, we had another bill before us which involved a subsidiary of this same company. That bill represented an attempt to kid the Canadian people that this company was the same old company with the same old name but not controlled by outside interests. It is not my intention to go over the memorandum again, but I suggest it shows what can be done and should be done. When any insurance bill goes through this house we should write in some safeguards. This should be the policy and intent of every member elected to the House of Commons, unless the
February 7, 1969

member is anxious to have Canada completely and thoroughly dominated by outside interests.
This memorandum is dated a couple of years ago. It refers to an insurance bill that was before this house. I think it is important for hon. members to know that bill was opposed by members of this house who argued that changes ought to be made. After a great deal of thought, we found that an agreement could be reached with this particular company. Canadians were going to have some control, and this control was written into the agreement. This is the type of thing we want. We want to write in safeguards when these bills come before parliament. There is absolutely no reason why safeguards cannot be written into these agreements. That is true of the particular bill before us.
The purpose of the incorporation sought by the earlier bill to which I have referred was the same as the purpose of incorporation in respect to the bill before us. The company was to be incorporated for the purpose of carrying on the business of life insurance in Canada. There is nothing wrong with that purpose. There are other parts of this agreement which I wish to leave with the members of this house for what I hope will be thoughtful consideration.
I am not going to read the entire context of this rather lengthy memorandum, but I will gladly provide a copy to anyone who wants it. It indicates that within two years of commencement of business, United Funds Management Ltd. would sell to officers, directors and employees of the company and, if necessary, others who are Canadian residents, 25 per cent of the capital stock of the insurance company for the original price. The memorandum goes on to suggest that within two years of the commencement of the business of this insurance company, it will offer Canadian residents a sufficient number of shares to bring its share ownership below 75 per cent. It says that within two years of the commencement of business the indirect ownership of Waddell and Reed will be reduced to a maximum of 56.25 per cent with practically all of the balance owned by residents of Canada.
Another paragraph of this memorandum indicates that United Funds Management Ltd. will undertake to sell to Canadian residents within ten years of the commencement of the business of the insurance company sufficient shares then owned by the insurance company

to bring the direct ownership of Waddell and Reed in the insurance company to below 50 per cent.
I am not going to go into the details, but this is supposed to provide an opportunity for Canadians to participate and eventually gain control of the company. There is absolutely nothing wrong with this idea and that is what members on this side of the house are very interested in assuring. We want to see moves made in this direction. As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) just pointed out, we have to make up our minds fairly soon as to what we intend to do in this connection.
Bills of this type should not be passed by this house unless we attach limiting restrictions. This is the forum in which to debate these issues. I for one would be extremely happy to hear members on the government side of the house defend this continuing sellout of Canadian industry and control to outside sources. Stand up in your seats and defend your positions, if this is government policy. We have seen too many instances where outside control has been disadvantageous to the nation. Either we take a stand very soon or it will be too late.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
We have been warned. We have had the Watkins report on foreign ownership which went into all phases of economic control. It touches every facet of the Canadian economy.
We come back to the financial institutions. In this area we have had some control over ownership, and I think it has been good. But anyone who tries to divorce insurance companies, and the terrific power they wield by reason of the tremendous portfolios of investment which they hold, from the financial field is very foolish indeed. We have talked in this house about investment in Canadian industry. Here is a source of funds for investment in Canadian industry. I suggest that it is essential to have the insurance industry under Canadian control. This does not mean wiping out all foreign insurance companies. There is a host of them in Canada now, and they take dividends out of this country and control to a very great extent their extensive portfolios of investment. We are losing the battle for Canadian control of industry in this country by continuing the type of legislation that is before us this afternoon. Before resuming my seat, Mr. Speaker, I have one or two more things to say on this bill. I have said before, and say again-

Hear, hear.

-that I do not think private members in this house should have the right to introduce this type of insurance bill. If it is government policy, the government should be in a position to advance this type of legislation. If the government favours the incorporation of these companies, it should say so; it should be part of the government's over-all program and policy. But the government does not do this. It tries to sneak in through the back door legislation of this type, hoping there will not be in the chamber enough members who wish to speak against this loss to the Canadian economy.
I believe several hon. members wish to speak on the bill. I would like, Mr. Speaker, to make my position very clear. As a Canadian, I am sick and tired of seeing the old line parties allowing the resources of this country to get out of the control of the Canadian people. We are paying for this policy. We see fabrication taking place in other nations, when the emphasis should be on fabrication taking place in our own country, thus giving jobs to Canadians in the Canadian setting. The people of this nation are gradually waking up and demanding that something be done in this respect. If the Liberal government does not do something to bring about the repatriation of some of the Canadian economy, it will be thrown out of power so quickly that it will make its head spin.
People hoped that a new direction would be taken by this government. I suggest that as far as industry is concerned the government should lay down a solid, sensible program of investment and control. Let us know where the government is going in this respect. I suggest it should start with very important industries, of which the insurance industry is one.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to state my views on this bill, in order to complete its consideration.
I think that Bill S-ll, as drawn up, is quite important. Like the previous speakers, I think that we are selling Canada piecemeal.
If we maintain that we must control our economy, those who are acquainted with the operations of the stock market and our economy will tell you that 69 per cent of our economy belongs to Americans and 31 per cent to Canadians.
This shows how healthy our administration has been, because we are selling Canada piecemeal.

We are now dealing with a big American company which wants to compete with other American and Canadian general insurance companies already in operation.
If my information is correct, in Canada there are about 292 companies selling insurance other than life insurance. Those American companies collect money in Canada for the benefit of the parent company established in the United States.
Someone wishes a child to be born in Canada, more precisely in Toronto, to collect money to be sent to the mother who lives in the United States. As an example, I will mention the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, which, on the one hand, invested 4 per cent of its assets in Canada in 1967-68, and on the other hand, made about 16 per cent of its revenue here.
You can see how profitable it is, and what happens when competition exists. The provinces pass legislation on crop insurance. The federal government and some provinces want to establish medicare. And now, bills are introduced authorizing American companies to open subsidiaries in Canada, naturally for the benefit of the United States.
It is not that I bear American investors a grudge, but I think it is time to take our economy in hand. Government members should ask economists to "rack their brains" in order to create the $5 million in credit which would enable the company involved to set up an organization which, thanks to the productiveness of its premiums, could invest again in Canada and enable Canadians to profit by the "revolving" money which would be invested in our private and public institutions.
I did not want to delay too much the discussion, but I think those considerations are very important. As the previous speakers said, in the field of mines, trade, industry and natural resources, we have already "Americanized" enough. When we speak of investment, it is not a time to create a "dumping" of money in favour of Americans, but rather to keep the ownership on our economy, in order to be able to say one day that we are a strong people.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately, I did not have the opportunity to prepare a speech on the bill before us.
I wish to welcome our new colleague the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin). Although he is not yet a member of the New
February 7, 1969

Democratic Party, maybe he will join our ranks before long.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

I want to take a few minutes to say something about Bill S-ll, to incorporate the Aetna Casualty Company of Canada. I took the opportunity to refer back to the minutes of proceedings of the Committee on Banking and Commerce of last October 23, at which time the subject matter of this Bill S-ll was before hon. Senators in the other place. It would seem that what is involved here is an attempt on the part of the Aetna Casualty Company to change the mode of operation of its Canadian branch and to change the form of incorporation. Rather than operate in Canada in the future as a branch of a U.S. company, it seeks now to become incorporated as a Canadian company. But it is interesting to note that even though the company will be registered as a Canadian company, and operating under Canadian law, it will still be owned in very large part, if not exclusively, by the U.S. parent company which goes by the same name.
It is also interesting to note that, according to the Financial Times of last year, the United States parent company is now facing litigation in the United States on anti-trust charges. Of course, one might argue that this problem of litigation facing the parent firm has nothing to do with the bill that is before us, but I think there is some relationship. It is certainly a point which hon. members should take into account when considering the pros and cons of Bill S-ll, preliminary to deciding how they will actually vote on the bill.
Some hon. members might think that this is a very routine proceeding in which we are engaged, that some private member is simply sponsoring a bill to incorporate an insurance company or to change its charter. However, I suggest that it is not routine. There are many ramifications and implications for the whole Canadian economy. We know that insurance companies take their premium income and invest it in the economy, and that is fine. But we do not know specifically to what extent Canadian premium insurance dollars are being collected in Canada and invested abroad.
I suspect that the trend in the last four or five years has been a rather dramatic increase in the amount of Canadian insurance premium dollars collected from Canadians here and
Private Bills
invested outside the country. Certainly, in February and March of 1967 there was a dramatic increase in the outflow of Canadian insurance premium dollars which were invested in the United States by companies operating here. So dramatic was this increase in February, March and April of 1967 that even our financial journals, such as the Financial Post and Financial Times were moved to comment about it on more than one occasion. We are often told that one of the great problems in our country is the reluctance on the part of Canadians to invest in risk enterprises. Sometimes we are presented with such a bald statement. The fact of the matter is that there would be much more investment by Canadians if there was a greater availability of stocks for purchase, and if Canadian insurance premium dollars were directed to investment in Canada.
I believe it is fair to say that very often potential Canadian1 investors cannot find an adequate supply of public stock. I know this might sound a little hard to believe but I think it is being said with more and more frequency, that there is actually a scarcity of public stocks on the market relative to the availability of investment capital. This is completely contrary to the conventional belief of the past decade that there is an under supply of Canadian investment capital. The situation seems to be exactly the reverse of what we are so often told.
I took a couple of minutes to make that point because it relates to the operation of insurance companies here in Canada. I noticed news items in the Ottawa Journal issues of February 5 and 6. These articles stated that in the Canadian insurance industry there has been quite a bit of activity lately and that some insurance companies have been engaged in take-over bids of other insurance companies. Apparently this has resulted in a rapid increase in share trading on the stock exchange in insurance company stocks. One is curious as to why Canadian insurance companies should, all of a sudden, be engaged in such takeover bids and stock market shenanigans. Certainly, this is what appears to be the case. There must be something of immediate private interest to insurance companies to cause them to change their articles of incorporation and their form of organization and operation. There must be some advantage to them ini wishing to split their shares. All of these things make it a little easier for insurance companies to manipulate and manoeu-ver in subscribing for capital, and make it

Private Bills
easier for them to operate on the stock market. I do not know of what benefit this can be to the public interest or to the national economy as a whole. We do know that foreign investment in Canada has been a growing problem in the post-war decade. One or two Liberal cabinet ministers were brought to the point of stating it had become a matter of urgent national interest great enough to necessitate the appointment of a special commission to study it.
On reading the report of the Watkins commission and its recommendations, we find that indeed the problem of foreign ownership has increased drastically in our time. The prospects are that the problem will linger with us and get worse in the years ahead unless some concerted effort is made by the government to treat the problem of ever increasing foreign ownership of our natural riches and resources1. So far, we have not had an indication from the government as to what it intends to do with respect to this specific and concrete problem. The validity of the words1 spoken by my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) is fortified. He is suggesting to hon. members that it is not too late now for us to insist that the government have a policy and an attitude with respect to private bills which come before us week after week asking for the incorporation of new financial institutions and for a change in the mode of operation of insurance companies.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I do not think it is enough that bills of this kind should be introduced by private members and voted on by the small handful of members in the house at the time with the government adopting no attitude whatever toward them. I am sure that 30 or 40 years ago the government would have adopted a position of respectful neutrality toward private bills praying for the incorporation of financial houses or insurance companies. However, I do not think that sort of attitude is any longer valid, simply because the amount of capital accumulated by insurance companies in premium form has increased greatly in the past decade. It therefore follows that the amount of investment capital that insurance companies are able to marshal and invest in the way they so choose has a very direct and substantial effect on our entire national economic performance.
Let us look at the performance of insurance companies in Canada during the year 1967. In

that year insurance companies invested something like 40 per cent of their investment portfolios in mortgages on real estate and homes. There is nothing wrong with this; indeed one hopes they will make even more of their investment portfolios available for mortgages, and in that way help play their part in solving the rather grave problem created by the housing shortgage in this country.
At the same time, these insurance companies have been rather pleased with the way they have been able to escalate the interest rate on mortgages accepted by them on real estate and homes. For example, the interest rate charged by insurance companies on mortgages all through the 1950's was of the order of 4 per cent, 4.3 per cent, 4.5 per cent and 4.6 per cent. By the early 1960's it had reached the 5 per cent level. However, in the past two years interest rates on mortgages in Canada have increased so greatly and irrationally that one can only say that these rates have run amok since early 1967.
The fact that insurance companies do have a large volume of capital available for mortgage investment has not seemed to make any difference to these rates. Therefore, I conclude that insurance companies operating in Canada have not been motivated by any desire to do what they can to hold the line on interest rates in this country. They have been as anxious as the rest, if not more so, to see interest rates escalate. Since nearly half of their investment portfolio is in the form of mortgages, the higher the interest rate, the better they like it.

I understand the President of the Privy Council has an announcement to make.
